interfaces.name: Scalar BEKK model
interfaces.type_shape: Conditional covariance recursion with a fixed unconditional covariance matrix. Dimension-dependent coefficients are supplied by Section 2.1. No simulation-specific population covariance or stationary initialization is added.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Conditional covariance recursion with a fixed unconditional covariance matrix. Dimension-dependent coefficients are supplied by Section 2.1. No simulation-specific population covariance or stationary initialization is added.

members.statement_original:
In particular, the widely used scalar BEKK model describes the dynamics of covariance matrix as follows:
\[
\boldsymbol\Sigma_{t+1}=(1-a-b)\overline{\boldsymbol\Sigma}+a\mathbf R_t\mathbf R_t^T+b\boldsymbol\Sigma_t,\tag{1.1}
\]
where $\overline{\boldsymbol\Sigma}$ is the unconditional covariance matrix, $\boldsymbol\Sigma_t$ is the conditional covariance matrix of the returns $\mathbf R_t=(R_{1t},\ldots,R_{pt})^T$, and $0\le a,b\le1$ with $a+b<1$ are related parameters. The parameter $a$ is sometimes referred to as the innovation coefficient, and $a+b$ the persistence coefficient.

interfaces.name: Returns
interfaces.type_shape: Returns obtained by the positive semidefinite covariance square root acting on iid standardized vectors. Gaussianity is imposed separately in Assumption 1.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Returns obtained by the positive semidefinite covariance square root acting on iid standardized vectors. Gaussianity is imposed separately in Assumption 1.

members.statement_original: Under a dynamic volatility model, returns are modeled as $\mathbf R_t=(\boldsymbol\Sigma_t)^{1/2}\mathbf z_t$, where $\mathbf z_t=(z_{1t},\ldots,z_{pt})^T$ are i.i.d. with mean zero and covariance matrix $\mathbf I$.

interfaces.name: I.i.d.
interfaces.type_shape: Coupled iid comparison sample using the unconditional covariance square root. The source writes the endpoint T here, while the sample covariance below sums to n; no identification is silently inserted.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Coupled iid comparison sample using the unconditional covariance square root. The source writes the endpoint T here, while the sample covariance below sums to n; no identification is silently inserted.

members.statement_original: Define $\mathbf R_t^0=(\overline{\boldsymbol\Sigma})^{1/2}\mathbf z_t$, $t=1,\ldots,T$, which share the same unconditional covariance matrix as $\mathbf R_t$ but are i.i.d..

interfaces.name: Sample covariance matrices
interfaces.type_shape: Pair of uncentered sample second-moment matrices normalized by n, with descending eigenvalues. These are two distinct sample objects, not independent samples or sample-mean-centered estimators.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Pair of uncentered sample second-moment matrices normalized by n, with descending eigenvalues. These are two distinct sample objects, not independent samples or sample-mean-centered estimators.

members.statement_original:
Denote the corresponding sample covariance matrices by
\[
\mathbf S_n=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbf R_t\mathbf R_t^T,\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbf S_n^0=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbf R_t^0(\mathbf R_t^0)^T.
\]
We write $\widehat\lambda_1\ge\ldots\ge\widehat\lambda_p$ as the eigenvalues of $\mathbf S_n$, and $\widehat\lambda_1^0\ge\ldots\ge\widehat\lambda_p^0$ as the eigenvalues of $\mathbf S_n^0$.

interfaces.name: Empirical spectral distribution
interfaces.type_shape: Equal-weight empirical distribution function of all p eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix, including zero eigenvalues.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Equal-weight empirical distribution function of all p eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix, including zero eigenvalues.

members.statement_original: For any symmetric matrix $\mathbf A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p$, its empirical spectral distribution (ESD) is defined as $F^{\mathbf A}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^p\mathbf1_{[\lambda_j,+\infty)}(x)/p$, $x\in\mathbb R$.

interfaces.name: Assumption 1
interfaces.type_shape: Four-part sequence-level assumption: iid Gaussian innovations, nondegenerate limiting population ESD on the nonnegative half-line, uniformly bounded population spectral norm, and positive limiting dimension/sample-size ratio. Parts (i)–(iv) are all preserved; no finite-dimensional lower eigenvalue bound is added.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Four-part sequence-level assumption: iid Gaussian innovations, nondegenerate limiting population ESD on the nonnegative half-line, uniformly bounded population spectral norm, and positive limiting dimension/sample-size ratio. Parts (i)–(iv) are all preserved; no finite-dimensional lower eigenvalue bound is added.

members.statement_original:
(i) $\mathbf z_t\underset{i.i.d.}{\sim}N(0,\mathbf I)$.

(ii) $\overline{\boldsymbol\Sigma}$ is nonnegative definite and its ESD, $F^{\overline{\boldsymbol\Sigma}}$, converges in distribution to a probability distribution $H$ on $[0,\infty)$ as $p\to\infty$, and $H\ne\delta(0)$, the Dirac measure at $0$.

(iii) $\|\overline{\boldsymbol\Sigma}\|<C$ for some constant $C>0$.

(iv) The dimension $p$ and the sample size $n$ satisfy that $p,n\to\infty$, and $p/n\to y>0$.

interfaces.name: Spectral norm
interfaces.type_shape: Euclidean operator norm of a real matrix, with the source maximum over the closed unit ball.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Euclidean operator norm of a real matrix, with the source maximum over the closed unit ball.

members.statement_original: For any matrix $\mathbf A=(A_{ij})$, its spectral norm is defined as $\|\mathbf A\|=\max_{\|\mathbf x\|\le1}\sqrt{\mathbf x^T\mathbf A^T\mathbf A\mathbf x}$, where $\|\mathbf x\|=\sqrt{\sum x_i^2}$ for any vector $\mathbf x=(x_i)$;

interfaces.name: Frobenius norm
interfaces.type_shape: Unnormalized real-matrix Frobenius norm. Theorem 5 places the factor p^{-1/2} outside this norm.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Unnormalized real-matrix Frobenius norm. Theorem 5 places the factor p^{-1/2} outside this norm.

members.statement_original: the Frobenius norm is defined as $\|\mathbf A\|_F=\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}^2}$.

interfaces.name: Levy distance
interfaces.type_shape: Levy distance between real distribution functions, using two horizontal/vertical epsilon shifts. This is not Wasserstein distance or uniform CDF distance.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Levy distance between real distribution functions, using two horizontal/vertical epsilon shifts. This is not Wasserstein distance or uniform CDF distance.

members.statement_original:
Recall that for any two distributions $F_1$ and $F_2$, the Levy distance between them is defined as
\[
L(F_1,F_2):=\inf\{\varepsilon>0|F_1(x-\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\le F_2(x)\le F_1(x+\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\text{ for all }x\in\mathbb R\}.
\]

interfaces.name: Reducible case
interfaces.type_shape: Vanishing eta regime for dimension-dependent BEKK coefficients. The scalar function eta is separately transcribed from (2.1) in ambient passage A3; its exact square-root scaling is retained.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Vanishing eta regime for dimension-dependent BEKK coefficients. The scalar function eta is separately transcribed from (2.1) in ambient passage A3; its exact square-root scaling is retained.

members.statement_original: We refer to the case when $\eta(a_p,b_p,p)\to0$ as the reducible case.

interfaces.name: Non-reducible case
interfaces.type_shape: Eta bounded away from zero, instantiated in Theorem 2 as eta>c for a fixed positive constant. This is distinct from the vanishing regime; eta itself is defined in ambient passage A3.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Eta bounded away from zero, instantiated in Theorem 2 as eta>c for a fixed positive constant. This is distinct from the vanishing regime; eta itself is defined in ambient passage A3.

members.statement_original: We refer to the case when $\eta(a_p,b_p,p)$ is bounded away from zero as the non-reducible case.

interfaces.name: Second moment
interfaces.type_shape: Random second moments of two empirical eigenvalue distributions, normalized by p. Theorem 2 compares their expectations, not a samplewise order.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Random second moments of two empirical eigenvalue distributions, normalized by p. Theorem 2 compares their expectations, not a samplewise order.

members.local_label: Section 2.2.2 — second moments of the ESDs
members.source_heading: Section 2.2.2 — second moments of the ESDs
members.statement_original:
We measure the difference in the ESD's between the BEKK model and the practically relevant i.i.d. case by the second moment of the ESD's:
\[
M_2=M_2^p=\sum_{i=1}^p\widehat\lambda_i^2/p=\operatorname{tr}\big((\mathbf S_n)^2\big)/p,\quad\text{and}\quad M_2^0=M_2^{0,p}=\sum_{i=1}^p(\widehat\lambda_i^0)^2/p=\operatorname{tr}\big((\mathbf S_n^0)^2\big)/p.
\]

interfaces.name: Univariate GARCH model
interfaces.type_shape: Coordinate GARCH variance recursion with the shared BEKK coefficients. Unconditional marginal variance is overbar-sigma squared, not time-dependent sigma squared.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Coordinate GARCH variance recursion with the shared BEKK coefficients. Unconditional marginal variance is overbar-sigma squared, not time-dependent sigma squared.

members.statement_original:
Under the BEKK model (1.1), the time-variation in the covariance matrix is governed by the two coefficients, $a_p$ and $b_p$, and each $R_{it}$ follows a univariate GARCH model:
\[
\sigma_{i,t+1}^2=(1-a_p-b_p)\overline\sigma_i^2+a_pR_{it}^2+b_p\sigma_{i,t}^2,\tag{2.4}
\]
where $\sigma_{i,t}^2=(\boldsymbol\Sigma_t)_{ii}$, and $\overline\sigma_i^2=(\overline{\boldsymbol\Sigma})_{ii}$ for $1\le i\le p$.

interfaces.name: QMLE
interfaces.type_shape: Randomly selected single-coordinate Gaussian quasi-likelihood fit, including its constrained parameter space. The positive objective is printed with argmax, not argmin; initialization and tie selection are not specified here.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Randomly selected single-coordinate Gaussian quasi-likelihood fit, including its constrained parameter space. The positive objective is printed with argmax, not argmin; initialization and tie selection are not specified here.

members.statement_original:
Specifically, we randomly select one variable, say, $i_0$, fit a univariate GARCH model to $(R_{i_0t})$ and get QMLE $\widehat a$ and $\widehat b$:
\[
(\widehat a,\widehat b,\widehat{\overline\sigma}_{i_0})=\operatorname*{argmax}_{(a,b,\overline\sigma_{i_0})\in\Omega}\frac1n\left(\sum_{t=1}^n\left(\frac{R_{i_0t}^2}{\sigma_{i_0t}^2}+\log(\sigma_{i_0t}^2)\right)\right),
\]
where $\Omega=\{(a,b,\overline\sigma),0\le a\le1,0\le b\le1,a+b\le1-\delta,\delta\le\overline\sigma^2<C\}$ for some positive constants $\delta$ and $C$.
members.variant_note: The source prints argmax of a positive sum of standardized squared returns plus log variance. This transcription does not change its sign or optimization direction.

interfaces.name: Projection matrix
interfaces.type_shape: Positive regularized lag-weighted return matrix with an identity term and estimated coefficients. The author calls it a projection matrix; orthogonal projection or idempotence is not asserted. The asymptotic lag-count condition is kept.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Positive regularized lag-weighted return matrix with an identity term and estimated coefficients. The author calls it a projection matrix; orthogonal projection or idempotence is not asserted. The asymptotic lag-count condition is kept.

members.statement_original:
We then use $\widehat a$, $\widehat b$ and past returns to construct a projection matrix:
\[
\mathbf P_t=\frac{1-\widehat a-\widehat b+\widehat a\widehat b^{M_p}}{1-\widehat b}\mathbf I+\sum_{j=1}^{M_p}\widehat a\widehat b^{j-1}\mathbf R_{t-j}\mathbf R_{t-j}^T,\tag{2.5}
\]
where $M_p$ represents the number of lagged returns included in $\mathbf P_t$, which grows with $p$ and $M_p=o(\sqrt p)$.

interfaces.name: Time-variation adjusted returns
interfaces.type_shape: Inverse-square-root transformation of dynamic returns, not a scalar rescaling or orthogonal projection.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Inverse-square-root transformation of dynamic returns, not a scalar rescaling or orthogonal projection.

members.statement_original: To be more precise, using the projection matrix $\mathbf P_t$, we define the time-variation adjusted returns $\widetilde{\mathbf R}_t=\mathbf P_t^{-1/2}\mathbf R_t$,

interfaces.name: Time-variation adjusted (TV-adj) sample covariance matrix
interfaces.type_shape: Uncentered covariance of inverse-square-root-adjusted returns, normalized by n. It remains random and is not asserted to have independent observations.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Uncentered covariance of inverse-square-root-adjusted returns, normalized by n. It remains random and is not asserted to have independent observations.

members.statement_original:
and the time-variation adjusted (TV-adj) sample covariance matrix:
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf S}_n=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n\widetilde{\mathbf R}_t(\widetilde{\mathbf R}_t)^T.\tag{2.6}
\]

interfaces.name: Stieltjes transform
interfaces.type_shape: Limiting sample spectral law specified by its upper-half-plane Stieltjes transform and the printed Marchenko–Pastur equation. The preceding convergence statement is context, not a theorem assumption or a dependency on a particular estimator implementation. Equation (2.9) uses y, unlike y^{-1} in Theorem 4.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Limiting sample spectral law specified by its upper-half-plane Stieltjes transform and the printed Marchenko–Pastur equation. The preceding convergence statement is context, not a theorem assumption or a dependency on a particular estimator implementation. Equation (2.9) uses y, unlike y^{-1} in Theorem 4.

members.local_label: Section 2.3 — limiting spectral law and transform (2.8)–(2.9)
members.source_heading: Section 2.3 — limiting spectral law and transform (2.8)–(2.9)
members.statement_original:
and $F$ is determined by that its Stieltjes transform
\[
m_F(z):=\int_{\lambda\in\mathbb R}\frac1{\lambda-z}\,dF(\lambda),\ z\in\mathbb C^+:=\{z\in\mathbb C,\operatorname{Im}(z)>0\}\tag{2.8}
\]
solves the following equation
\[
m_F(z)=\int_{\tau\in\mathbb R}\frac1{\tau\left(1-y\left(1+zm_F(z)\right)\right)-z}\,dH(\tau).\tag{2.9}
\]

interfaces.name: Bounded function
interfaces.type_shape: Spectral application of the bounded function g to the population covariance. Population eigenvalues lambda_i^H are identified on page 10 and archived as ambient context; this is not the normalized generalized ESD.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Spectral application of the bounded function g to the population covariance. Population eigenvalues lambda_i^H are identified on page 10 and archived as ambient context; this is not the normalized generalized ESD.

members.statement_original: for some bounded function $g(\cdot)$, and $g(\overline{\boldsymbol\Sigma})=\sum_{i=1}^p g(\lambda_i^H)\mathbf v_i\mathbf v_i^T$, where $\mathbf v_i$'s are the eigenvectors of $\overline{\boldsymbol\Sigma}$.

interfaces.name: Generalized Stieltjes transform
interfaces.type_shape: Population-weighted resolvent trace divided by p. This normalization differs from the trace(g(Sigma)) denominator in the preceding generalized ESD (2.10); do not silently identify it with that normalized distribution Stieltjes transform.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Population-weighted resolvent trace divided by p. This normalization differs from the trace(g(Sigma)) denominator in the preceding generalized ESD (2.10); do not silently identify it with that normalized distribution Stieltjes transform.

members.statement_original:
Parallel to the i.i.d. case, we study the limiting property of the generalized ESD of the TV-adj sample covariance matrix via the following generalized Stieltjes transform:
\[
\Theta_n^g(z)=\frac1p\operatorname{tr}\left((\widetilde{\mathbf S}_n-z\mathbf I)^{-1}g(\overline{\boldsymbol\Sigma})\right).\tag{2.11}
\]

interfaces.name: Truncation
interfaces.type_shape: Upper clipping at a large fixed constant L, with the eigenvectors preserved. Tau is a superscript label and is not an independently specified threshold. A lower clipping threshold is not introduced.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Upper clipping at a large fixed constant L, with the eigenvectors preserved. Tau is a superscript label and is not an independently specified threshold. A lower clipping threshold is not introduced.

members.statement_original: where $\widetilde{\mathbf S}_n^\tau=\sum_{i=1}^p\widetilde\lambda_i^\tau\widetilde{\mathbf u}_i\widetilde{\mathbf u}_i^T$, $\widetilde\lambda_i^\tau=\min(\widetilde\lambda_i,L)$, and $L$ is a large constant. The truncation is applied to ensure that the support of the ESD is bounded.

interfaces.name: TV-adj nonlinear shrinkage estimator
interfaces.type_shape: Output of the Ledoit–Wolf (2015) nonlinear shrinkage algorithm on the truncated adjusted covariance. The main text does not supply the full external algorithm; preserve this unresolved construction rather than substitute the displayed population oracle.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Output of the Ledoit–Wolf (2015) nonlinear shrinkage algorithm on the truncated adjusted covariance. The main text does not supply the full external algorithm; preserve this unresolved construction rather than substitute the displayed population oracle.

members.statement_original: Specifically, to estimate the unconditional covariance matrix, we perform the nonlinear shrinkage algorithm by Ledoit and Wolf (2015) on $\widetilde{\mathbf S}_n^\tau$, where $\widetilde{\mathbf S}_n^\tau=\sum_{i=1}^p\widetilde\lambda_i^\tau\widetilde{\mathbf u}_i\widetilde{\mathbf u}_i^T$, $\widetilde\lambda_i^\tau=\min(\widetilde\lambda_i,L)$, and $L$ is a large constant. The truncation is applied to ensure that the support of the ESD is bounded. We denote by $\widetilde{\boldsymbol\Sigma}$ the resulting covariance matrix estimator, which we call the TV-adj nonlinear shrinkage estimator (TV-adj NLS).

interfaces.name: Infeasible oracle shrinkage estimator
interfaces.type_shape: Population-law-dependent oracle with a separate zero-eigenvalue branch for y>1. Preserve the source ordinary square, underlined companion F, and unindexed boundary-value shorthand. External results justify its optimality but are not extra statement prerequisites.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Population-law-dependent oracle with a separate zero-eigenvalue branch for y>1. Preserve the source ordinary square, underlined companion F, and unindexed boundary-value shorthand. External results justify its optimality but are not extra statement prerequisites.

members.statement_original:
Define $\widetilde{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{or}=\sum_{i=1}^p d_i^{or}(\widetilde\lambda_i^\tau)\widetilde{\mathbf u}_i\widetilde{\mathbf u}_i^T$, where
\[
d_i^{or}(\widetilde\lambda_i^\tau)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac1{(y-1)\check m_{\underline F}(0)}&\text{if }\widetilde\lambda_i^\tau=0\text{ and }y>1,\\\displaystyle\frac{\widetilde\lambda_i^\tau}{\left(1-y-y\widetilde\lambda_i^\tau\cdot\check m_F(\widetilde\lambda_i^\tau)\right)^2}&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\quad\text{for }i=1,\ldots,p,\tag{2.13}
\]
$m_{\underline F}=(y-1)/z+ym_F(z)$, $\underline F(x)=(1-y)\mathbf1_{\{[0,\infty)\}}(x)+yF(x)$, $\check m(\lambda)=\lim_{z\in\mathbb C^+\to\lambda}m_F(z)$, $F(\cdot)$ and $m_F(z)$ are given in (2.8) and (2.9), respectively. By Theorem 4 and Theorem 4 of Ledoit and Péché (2011), $\widetilde{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{or}$ is the infeasible oracle shrinkage estimator.
members.variant_note: The positive-eigenvalue denominator is printed as an ordinary square, with no modulus bars. The source also leaves the F subscript off the left side of its boundary-value definition. These formulas are retained without correction.
